newsitem.title: UK: LatAm stocks outstrip Asia, E.Europe in New Year.
newsitem.headline: LatAm stocks outstrip Asia, E.Europe in New Year.

text.p: Latin America powered into the New Year staging an impressive stock market rally that has so far left Asia and emerging Europe, the Middle East and Africa in the shade, fund managers said on Tuesday. Rallies in Mexico, Chile and Brazil drove Latin America up 1.8 percent on the International Finance Corp's (IFC) composite index of emerging market equities -- one of the main means which fund managers use as a benchmark of portfolio performance.
The figures after the first full trading day of 1997 contrast with rises of just 0.4 percent in Asia and 0.3 percent in Europe, Middle East and Africa.
ING Barings Emerging Market Index corroborated the IFC's results, showing Latin America surging 2.02 percent against 0.01 in Asia and 0.21 in Europe.
Emily McLaughlin, Latin America fund manager at Foreign & Colonial, said that while F&C saw markets of value in Asia and eastern Europe, the Latin American story was highly persuasive.

"There are compelling reasons why you'd want to look at Latin America as a region," she said, pointing to falling inflation, rising GDP growth, increasing foreign reserves, falling debt servicing ratios and budgets well within Europe's Maastricht criteria -- a byword for economic discipline.
Analysts expect Latin America to offer earnings per share growth of around 17 percent in 1997 on an average multiple of 11, while Asia will offer about 11 percent on a multiple of around 16.
"You have higher earnings growth and are paying less for it in Latin America," McLaughlin said.

David Lubin, economic adviser for emerging markets at HSBC, agreed Latin America's fundamentals looked good, especially in comparison with some Asian markets beset by unsustainable rates of GDP growth and weak export earnings.

But he stressed there were rallies in selected emerging markets across the globe on Monday, including the Czech Republic, Hungary, Turkey and Indonesia, and the current surges may be a repeat of last year's New Year flurry.
Latin America, however, may still have more to offer investors than troubled economies such as the Czech Republic, Poland, Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia.

"Latin America, although it has shaken off much of the burden that accumulated as a result of the Mexican crisis, is still in the process of reestablishing credibility and investors can take advantage of that," Lubin said.

However Lee Chautin, head of ING Barings's emerging market index, said a two percent rally was not unusual in markets as volatile as these, shown in annual volatility of 14.37 percent for Latin America against 11.90 for emerging Europe and Asia's 10.36 percent.

Austin Forey, who manages half a billion dollars in emerging market funds for Flemings Investment Management, said the Latin American rally was sparked in part by asset allocation decisions made at the end of last year.
But he added that as far as Flemings was concerned, Latin America and Asia have been benefitting from a shift in weightings out of eastern Europe.
"We have been very overweight in eastern Europe throughout 1996, although we have (since) been scaling back. That money is going into Latin America and into Asia," he said.
